whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the B2B Solution Architect exam for?

personas.label: Hands-on practitioners
personas.description: You have built Sales Cloud, Service Cloud or CPQ solutions for B2B companies and want to show you can design across all of them.

personas.label: Solution designers
personas.description: You lead discovery and solution design on projects where several Salesforce clouds and outside systems have to work together.

personas.label: Career builders
personas.description: You are moving from a single-cloud consultant role into a cross-cloud architect role.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the B2B Solution Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a hard exam because it is wide. One question might be about the data model across clouds, the next about integration with an ERP, and the next about how to run the project. Real project experience helps more than memorising features.
bullets: 60 scored multiple-choice questions, plus a few unscored ones.
About 63% to pass, about 38 correct answers out of 60. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book, since Salesforce updates these.
Cross-cloud scenarios. Expect questions that mix Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, CPQ, Order Management, B2B Commerce and Experience Cloud.
Project delivery counts. Some questions are about discovery, governance and change management, not just technology.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People with several years of solution design work on B2B projects tend to do best. Before you book, aim for 75% or more on practice tests and make sure you can explain how a quote turns into an order and an invoice across your systems.

examFormat.heading: B2B Solution Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a B2B company with a specific problem, such as slow quoting or customer data spread across systems, and ask which design solves it best.
bestWayToPass: Follow the B2B process end to end: Lead, opportunity, quote, order, fulfilment, invoice and service. Know which cloud or system owns each step.
Know where data should live: Decide which system is the source of truth for accounts, products, prices and orders.
Learn the integration basics: When to use real-time APIs, events or batch loads between Salesforce and an ERP.
Don't skip delivery topics: Discovery, requirements, governance and adoption all show up.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you design B2B solutions that span several Salesforce clouds and outside systems. You decide where data lives, how systems connect, and how the project is run.

keyConcepts.h2: B2B Solution Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Solution Architecture Fundamentals
blocks.body: A B2B solution architect starts with the business process, not the product list. Map the steps from first contact to renewal, find the pain points, and only then decide which cloud handles each step. A common B2B flow is: Sales Cloud for leads and opportunities, CPQ or Revenue Cloud for quotes, Order Management or the ERP for orders, the ERP for invoicing, and Service Cloud for support. Experience Cloud or B2B Commerce lets customers and partners serve themselves. Prefer standard features and configuration over custom code, because they are cheaper to run and upgrade.

blocks.heading: Multi-Cloud Data Architecture
blocks.body: Every key piece of data needs one system that owns it, called the source of truth. Customer accounts often live in Salesforce. Products and prices may be owned by the ERP and copied in. Orders may start in Salesforce and be finished in the ERP. Use **external IDs** to match the same record across systems, and keep the Account and Contact model simple so every cloud can share it. Watch for large data volumes on objects like Orders and Assets, and plan archiving. **Data Cloud** can bring customer data from many sources into one profile without moving everything into the core org.

blocks.heading: Integration Architecture Patterns
blocks.body: B2B projects nearly always connect to an ERP. Use real-time API calls only when a user is waiting, such as checking stock or credit during quoting. Use **Platform Events** or **Change Data Capture** when other systems just need to know something changed, like a closed opportunity. Use batch loads with Bulk API for large nightly syncs such as price lists. When several systems share the same data, middleware such as MuleSoft keeps the connections in one place and makes them reusable.

blocks.heading: Security & Compliance Design
blocks.body: B2B customers and partners often log in to the same org through Experience Cloud. Plan sharing so each company sees only its own accounts, orders and cases. Use account relationships or sharing sets for external users. Think about data residency, consent and privacy rules such as GDPR when customer data crosses borders or systems. Use single sign-on for employees and, where it helps, for partners. Shield encryption and Event Monitoring may be needed in regulated industries.

blocks.heading: Governance, Change Management & Scalability
blocks.body: Large B2B programmes touch many teams, so governance matters. Set up a design authority that approves big decisions, clear standards for naming and code, and a release plan with the right sandboxes. Run discovery workshops with the business before designing. Plan training and adoption early, since a good design that nobody uses still fails. Design for growth: more users, more orders and more countries should not need a rebuild.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce B2B Solution Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions give you a B2B company, a problem and several reasonable designs. Pick the one that solves the stated problem with the least custom work and a clear owner for each piece of data.

blocks.heading: Multi-Cloud B2B Architecture
blocks.body: Match each step of the B2B process to the cloud or system that owns it. Questions often hide the answer in which step is causing the pain.

blocks.heading: B2B Data Model Design
blocks.body: Keep one shared Account model. Decide which system owns products, prices and orders, and use external IDs to keep them in sync.

blocks.heading: Integration Architecture for B2B
blocks.body: Real time when a user waits, events when others just need to know, batch for big scheduled loads. Middleware once several systems share data.

blocks.heading: CPQ for B2B Commerce
blocks.body: Quotes are usually built in CPQ or Revenue Cloud, then become orders. Know where pricing rules live and how the order reaches the ERP.

blocks.heading: Customer 360 for B2B
blocks.body: Customers and partners often need a portal. Experience Cloud or B2B Commerce lets them see orders, cases and invoices without calling support.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After B2B Solution Architect, many people move toward the platform architect credentials and CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: A manufacturer's sales reps wait two days for quotes because pricing rules live in spreadsheets kept by the finance team. What should the architect recommend first?
options: Build a custom Lightning component that reads the spreadsheet file each time
Move pricing and discounts into CPQ with approvals
Add more finance staff
Email the spreadsheet to reps every week
sampleQuestions.explanation: Putting pricing and approvals into the quoting tool lets reps build correct quotes themselves, with approvals only where needed.
whyWrong: A custom component on a spreadsheet is fragile and hard to maintain.
More staff treats the symptom and doesn't scale.
Weekly emails go out of date and reps still price by hand.

sampleQuestions.question: Product and price data is owned by the ERP, but reps quote in Salesforce. How should product data be handled?
options: Let the reps edit prices inside Salesforce and then copy them back into the ERP
Treat the ERP as source of truth and sync inwards
Ask reps to look up prices in the ERP for each quote
Keep two separate price lists and let reps choose
sampleQuestions.explanation: One system must own the data. If the ERP owns products and prices, Salesforce should receive copies and not change them.
whyWrong: Two-way editing causes conflicts and makes it unclear which price is right.
Looking up each price by hand is slow and causes mistakes.
Two price lists will drift apart and confuse everyone.

sampleQuestions.question: When a rep builds a quote, they must see live stock levels from the ERP before promising a delivery date. Which pattern fits?
options: A real-time request and reply call to the ERP
A Platform Event published when the quote is saved
A nightly batch sync of stock levels
A weekly export of stock data
sampleQuestions.explanation: The rep is waiting for the answer to make a promise, so a real-time call that returns current stock is the right fit.
whyWrong: A Platform Event doesn't return an answer to the rep.
Nightly data can be hours out of date.
Weekly data is far too old for delivery promises.

sampleQuestions.question: Several systems (ERP, billing, warehouse and a data lake) all need to know when an order is placed in Salesforce. What is the best design?
options: A nightly CSV export to each system
Four separate Apex callouts in the order trigger
Publish an event when an order is placed
Each system calls Salesforce every minute to check for new orders
sampleQuestions.explanation: Publishing one event lets every system react on its own. Salesforce doesn't need to know who is listening, and new subscribers can be added later.
whyWrong: Nightly exports are slow and need one integration per system.
Four callouts tie Salesforce to every system and fail if any one is down.
Constant polling wastes API calls and adds delay.

sampleQuestions.question: Partner companies log in to an Experience Cloud site to see their own orders. A partner must never see another partner's orders. What is the main design concern?
options: Sharing so external users see only their account
How many reports the partners can run
The page layout that is used by the internal users of the system
The colour scheme of the site
sampleQuestions.explanation: With many companies in one org, the sharing model is what keeps each partner's data separate. External defaults should be private, then opened up per account.
whyWrong: Report counts don't control record access.
Internal page layouts don't affect what partners can see.
Branding doesn't affect who can see data.

sampleQuestions.question: A B2B company wants a single view of each customer, but customer data sits in Salesforce, the ERP, a marketing tool and a support system. The core org shouldn't store everything. What fits?
options: Ask each team to update all four systems by hand
Use Data Cloud to unify the customer profiles
Pick one system and delete the others
Copy every system's data into custom objects
sampleQuestions.explanation: Data Cloud is designed to bring customer data from many sources together into unified profiles, without loading it all into the core CRM objects.
whyWrong: Manual updates in four systems never stay consistent.
Deleting systems that teams depend on isn't realistic.
Copying everything into custom objects bloats the org and is hard to keep in sync.

sampleQuestions.question: Where should an architect start when designing a new B2B solution?
options: Mapping the process and its pain points
Designing the page layouts
Writing the integration code
Choosing which of the Salesforce licences to buy
sampleQuestions.explanation: The process tells you what needs solving and which cloud or system should own each step. Products come after that.
whyWrong: Page layouts are a detail that depends on the process.
Code comes much later, after the design is agreed.
Licences depend on the design, so picking them first is backwards.

sampleQuestions.question: An order is captured in Salesforce, fulfilled in the ERP and then invoiced. Which statement is the best design principle?
options: Orders should be re-entered by hand in each system
Order data should only ever exist in Salesforce
Each step should have a clear owning system
Every system should be able to edit every order field
sampleQuestions.explanation: Clear ownership per step, linked by shared IDs, avoids conflicting edits and makes it easy to trace an order across systems.
whyWrong: Re-entering data by hand causes errors and delay.
The ERP needs the order to fulfil and invoice it.
Letting every system edit everything causes conflicts.

sampleQuestions.question: A global B2B company stores customer data for EU customers. What must the architect consider?
options: Only the speed of the website
Only the number of licences
Only the language of the user interface
Data privacy rules such as GDPR
sampleQuestions.explanation: Personal data of EU customers falls under GDPR. The design must handle consent, data access requests and where the data is held.
whyWrong: Speed matters, but it doesn't address legal duties.
Licence counts don't cover privacy.
Translation is useful, but it isn't a privacy control.

sampleQuestions.question: A programme has six delivery teams. Teams keep making conflicting design choices. What should the architect set up?
options: Let each team decide on its own
A design authority with standards and review
A rule stating that only one of the teams may work on it at a time
One huge release every year
sampleQuestions.explanation: A design authority and shared standards keep decisions consistent while teams work in parallel.
whyWrong: Working in isolation is what is causing the conflicts.
Only one team at a time would make delivery far too slow.
Yearly releases make each release riskier and slow down value.

sampleQuestions.question: Customers keep phoning support to ask about order status and download invoices. What is the best way to cut these calls?
options: Send each of the customers a spreadsheet once every week
Hire more support agents
Turn off the support phone line
A self-service portal for orders and invoices
sampleQuestions.explanation: A self-service portal through Experience Cloud or B2B Commerce lets customers check orders and invoices themselves at any time.
whyWrong: Spreadsheets go out of date and still cause questions.
More agents handle the same calls at higher cost.
Turning off support harms customers.

sampleQuestions.question: A business sponsor asks for a custom-built quoting engine. Standard CPQ meets 90% of the requirements. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use standard CPQ and cover the rest simply
Wait a year for new features
Use two separate quoting tools alongside one another
Build the custom engine
sampleQuestions.explanation: Standard features are cheaper to build, run and upgrade. The gap can often be closed with configuration or a small extension.
whyWrong: Waiting delays value when most needs are already met.
Two tools confuse users and duplicate data.
A custom engine is costly to build and maintain for a small gain.

sampleQuestions.question: Price list updates for 200,000 products come from the ERP once a night. Which approach fits?
options: A real-time callout for each product
A Platform Event per product
Batch load with Bulk API
Manual entry by the product team
sampleQuestions.explanation: Large, scheduled loads are what Bulk API is built for. It is efficient and uses few API calls.
whyWrong: 200,000 single calls would be slow and use up API limits.
Events per product add overhead for a simple nightly load.
Manual entry at this scale is not realistic.

sampleQuestions.question: A good design was delivered, but six months later few sales reps use it. What was most likely missed?
options: More custom code
A good many more fields added to the page
A bigger sandbox
Training, change management and adoption
sampleQuestions.explanation: Even good solutions fail without training and change management. Adoption should be planned from the start.
whyWrong: More code doesn't fix people not using the system.
Extra fields usually make adoption worse.
Sandbox size doesn't affect adoption.

sampleQuestions.question: The same customer appears in Salesforce and in the ERP with different IDs. How should the two be linked?
options: Match the records by customer name during a nightly batch job
Ask users to link them by hand
Store the ERP's ID in an external ID field in Salesforce
Keep them separate
sampleQuestions.explanation: An external ID field holds the other system's key, so integrations can match and upsert records reliably.
whyWrong: Names change and are not unique, so name matching causes errors.
Linking by hand is slow and error-prone.
Unlinked records mean no single view of the customer.
